tagline: Forest roads follow Lake Superior’s shore past a white brick lighthouse
intro: Whitefish Bay’s paved two-lane byway passes northern hardwoods, conifers and wetlands along Lake Superior’s shore. The Forest Service presents this National Forest Scenic Byway as a route through the lake’s natural beauty and cultural history, with waysides that reach the shoreline. Whitefish Bay also carries shipping traffic to and from the Soo Locks, with the international border running through its waters.

An earth road existed here by 1936, and gravel covered the full route by 1945. Paving began at the eastern end in the mid-1950s. Construction near Naomikong Point began in 1967 as part of a planned longer scenic highway connecting the Pictured Rocks area with Whitefish Bay and the St. Marys River. In the late 1970s, the western end was realigned closer to Tahquamenon Bay; the old roadway was removed. The last gap in the pavement closed in 1987, and National Forest Scenic Byway designation followed in 1989.

Start at M-123 south of Paradise and drive east through birch forest toward Tahquamenon Bay. Near Naomikong Point the road turns inland, then continues east along the shoreline toward Point Iroquois Lighthouse. Beyond the lighthouse, the route bends south toward the forest boundary west of Brimley. Bay Mills Indian Community lies immediately west of Brimley, whose waterfront faces Waiska Bay.

moments.title: Naomikong Point
moments.text: Part of Naomikong Point’s former occupation area now lies underwater just offshore. The point is a low meadow today, but it was pine forest when people used the site. Radiocarbon dating places occupation at some point between about 100 CE and 900 CE. Use was likely seasonal. Post molds thought to have supported fish-drying racks, together with other evidence, suggest heavy reliance on fishing. Archaeologists recovered more than 100,000 pottery fragments from at least 288 vessels. James Fitting surveyed the site in the 1960s, including an underwater investigation in 1964; Donald E. Janzen did further work in 1967.

moments.title: Point Iroquois Light
moments.text: The white brick lighthouse at Point Iroquois is the second light built here. Its predecessor began operating in 1856, but an inspector questioned its construction quality eleven years later. The first tower and keepers’ quarters were demolished, and the present light went up in 1870. It marks the meeting of Whitefish Bay and the western end of the St. Marys River. The station was deactivated in 1962, replaced by the Canadian-operated Gros Cap Reefs Light. Visitors can climb the tower, explore the boardwalk and see the visitor-center exhibits. The museum includes an apartment furnished to show the lightkeepers’ daily lives.
moments.notice: Notice the white brick tower at the boundary between Whitefish Bay and the St. Marys River.

moments.title: Bay Mills Indian Community
moments.text: Gnoozhekaaning, the Ojibwe name for Bay Mills Indian Community, means Place of the Pike. Bay Mills people have lived for hundreds of years along Whitefish Bay, the St. Marys River falls and the bluffs over Tahquamenon Bay. The community adopted a written constitution in 1937. Its work along these waters continues through the tribal Biological Services Department, whose programs include fisheries assessments, beach-health monitoring and water-quality studies. The tribe also operates Bay Mills Community College. Chartered by the community in 1984, the college grew from a vocational program serving the economic-development needs of seven Native American communities.
